richText.plainText: A vulnerability in which an attacker interferes with the SQL queries that an application sends to a database. If, as an attacker, you can interact with a query and modify it by adding SQL characters or code through the application's input vectors, the application is vulnerable.
— a login form with a username and password field, both of which end up in a query against the users table:
select * from users where username = 'admin'--' and password = '...'
If input is properly validated, the database looks for a literal username
, finds nothing, and the attacker gets an error
If the application is vulnerable (no parameterized queries, no input validation), the single quote closes the username string and the
comments out the rest of the query, so it becomes
is a real username, the database returns the administrator profile — the attacker is logged in as admin without ever knowing the password
This is SQL injection used to bypass authentication during login: the attacker didn't need to know the password, only how to change the query structure so the password check never runs.
Depends entirely on the context of the injection you're exploiting — some only let you view data, others let you modify it. Mapped to the CIA triad:
— viewing sensitive information such as usernames and passwords

— modifying data in the database. Real example: an application with a vulnerable "update your email" function let the author update another user's email to one they controlled, then use the forgotten-password flow to get the reset token sent to themselves — full account takeover
— that same integrity example also cost the victim access to their own account once the password was reset out from under them, so one exploited parameter hit all three at once

In some scenarios, SQL injection leads to remote code execution on the operating system — you inherit whatever privilege level the database process runs with, which is why least-privilege database configuration matters (see Prevention)

Judged loosely by the OWASP Top 10 — a community-maintained list of the 10 most critical web application security risks, revised every few years. Rankings shift a lot release to release (XSS went 2nd → 3rd → 7th; "Insufficient Transport Layer Protection" dropped off entirely once HTTPS became trivial to deploy; "Insecure Deserialization" appeared from nowhere in 2017). Injection has stayed in the

slot across every revision below — and while the likelihood of finding SQLi has gone down over the years (better frameworks, more awareness), the severity hasn't: one vulnerable parameter can still mean full remote code execution on the backend server.

SQL Injection
├── In-Band (Classic)       — same channel to launch attack and read result; easiest to exploit
│   ├── Error-based
│   └── Union-based
├── Inferential (Blind)     — no direct data transfer; inferred from app behavior; slower to exploit
│   ├── Boolean-based
│   └── Time-based
└── Out-of-Band             — data exfiltrated via a separate network channel (DNS/HTTP); uncommon
Some people lump Out-of-Band under "blind"/"inferential" too, which is fair — most references (and this guide) still split it out as its own category.

The attacker uses the same communication channel to both launch the attack and gather the result — the payload's output is presented directly in the application response, which is exactly why it's much easier to exploit than the blind categories: you see the result of your attack instead of having to infer it from behavior.
Forces the database to generate an error, which hands you information to refine the injection — different characters (
, etc.) surface different errors, and the goal is simply to trigger one.
You have an error in your SQL syntax, check the manual that corresponds to your MySQL server version…

The error message can reveal the database type, the version, and sometimes even the exact backend query being executed — if you get the exact query, you've hit the jackpot, because now you're building a payload against known structure instead of guessing it through trial and error

SQL operator to combine the results of two queries into one result set — instead of just returning whatever the original query returns, you get to also return the result of a query of your choosing (usernames/passwords, typically).
www.random.com/app.php?id=' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users--
below) — it's not "output whatever you want in as many fields as you want."

No actual data is transferred through the web application — the database never prints anything to the page. The attacker is forced to extract data by asking the database a series of yes/no questions and reading the application's behavior for the answer. Exploiting blind SQLi takes more time and skill than in-band, but it's
— you can still walk the database out one bit at a time.
Uses Boolean conditions to produce a different result depending on whether the query evaluates TRUE or FALSE. Also called content-based blind SQLi.
SELECT title FROM product WHERE id = 1
If the app responds differently to a forced-false vs. forced-true condition, it's vulnerable.
to pull one character out of the password at a time and compare it:
www.random.com/app.php?id=1 AND SUBSTRING((SELECT Password FROM Users WHERE Username = 'Administrator'), 1, 1) = 's'
www.random.com/app.php?id=1 AND SUBSTRING((SELECT Password FROM Users WHERE Username = 'Administrator'), 1, 1) = 'e'

Iterate through every alphanumeric character per position until you hit a TRUE, move to the next position, repeat — extracting the full hash this way can take thousands of queries, which is obviously not a manual job. Automate it: a Burp Intruder run, or a short Python script (~5-10 minutes to write) that asks the yes/no questions and reconstructs the string — the script itself then runs in under a minute.
Relies on the database pausing for a specified time, then returning, to signal a TRUE condition — used when there's no visible response difference to key off of (e.g.
Response takes 10 seconds → first letter IS
Response doesn't take 10 seconds (usually ~1s) → first letter is NOT
Logic: "if the first character of the administrator's hashed password is
Same extraction pattern as Boolean-based, just keyed off response
instead of response content — same need for a script that measures timing and infers true/false from it.

Triggers an out-of-band network connection to a system the attacker controls. Usually used when none of the other techniques apply — it depends on specific database features being enabled to establish a network connection, so it's not common.
Protocols: DNS and HTTP are the most commonly used
, hitting a Burp Collaborator-generated domain so the attacker controls it and can confirm any DNS lookups):

If a DNS/HTTP interaction is received, the vulnerability is confirmed. From there, some scenarios let you extract data directly; others still force you into the conditional yes/no pattern used for Boolean/time-based SQLi (query triggers a lookup → true; no lookup → false).
Methodology varies person to person and matures with experience — treat any given methodology (including this one) as a starting point to build on, not gospel. Split by testing perspective:
— minimal or no information beyond the application URL and scope
— full access to the system, including source code

(not always called out separately) — a middle ground, e.g. given login credentials but not source. For SQLi specifically, black-box and gray-box methodology end up being the same regardless of authentication state, so they're treated as one category here; white-box is genuinely different since it's code review, not black-box probing.

Walk every page reachable in your current user context, log every input vector that potentially talks to the backend, understand app logic, find subdomains/hidden directories — all while Burp's proxy silently captures every request. This step is underrated and arguably the

important one: skipping straight to throwing payloads at fields makes you functionally equivalent to a vulnerability scanner, which only ever catches the simplest bugs because it can't understand what the application is actually doing. The vulnerabilities worth finding are usually logic errors a scanner can't see, or hidden behind pages a scanner can't reach.
) and look for errors or other anomalies — errors are valuable because they tell you the database type/version, and sometimes the exact query, which massively narrows the payload-building work
) and look for differences in the application's responses
Submit payloads designed to trigger time delays and look for differences in response time
Submit OAST payloads designed to trigger an out-of-band network interaction, and monitor for interactions
The human advantage over a scanner: you can read the output and refine the payload iteratively toward a goal, instead of just flagging an anomaly

Enable web server logging and database logging first — logging turns the errors you'll trigger while fuzzing into confirmation you can check against the backend, and lets you verify (often ~90% confidence) that a parameter is vulnerable just from what got logged, before even opening the source

Map the application (visible functionality) same as black-box, then additionally regex-search the codebase for every place that talks to the database — this catches pages black-box mapping missed (not linked from the UI, not found by directory brute-forcing)
Fuzz as before, cross-check against the logs you enabled
When you suspect a function, review it end-to-end (e.g. the login function) until you've confirmed it's theoretically vulnerable, then confirm in practice by testing it directly

The number and order of columns must be the same in all queries
The data types must be compatible

order by 1--

The ORDER BY position number 3 is out of range of the number of items in the select list.
→ the column count is one less than the value that errored, so 2 columns
method — increment until an error appears:

' UNION SELECT NULL--                ← error
' UNION SELECT NULL, NULL--          ← no error → 2 columns confirmed
All queries combined using a UNION, INTERSECT or EXCEPT operator must have an equal number of expressions in their target lists.
values method — increment until no error appears:

' UNION SELECT 'a', NULL--   ← column 1 is not string (error)
' UNION SELECT NULL, 'a'--   ← column 2 is string ✓
Conversion failed when converting the varchar value 'a' to data type int.
Sometimes no column takes string data — that's a dead end for extracting text (you might still pull integers), and it comes down to the specific injection and context you're working in.
Find columns with a string-compatible data type
— probe each position with a string, since usernames/passwords are what you actually want and they're normally stored as strings:
www.random.com/app.php?id=' UNION SELECT username, password FROM users--
— put the real query in the string-compatible column(s):
Submit a Boolean condition that evaluates to FALSE and note the response
Submit a Boolean condition that evaluates to TRUE and note the response
If the two differ, write a program that asks the database a series of TRUE/FALSE questions via conditional statements and tracks the answers to reconstruct the target string
Submit a payload that pauses the application for a specified period of time and confirm the delay is real
Same as Boolean-based, but the script tracks response
instead of response content to infer true/false
Submit OAST payloads designed to trigger an out-of-band network interaction and monitor for resulting interactions
Depending on the injection point, either extract data directly, or fall back to the conditional yes/no pattern (interaction received = true, no interaction = false)

— open source, the most well-known dedicated SQLi tool. Highly customizable: choose the injection parameter, testing intensity, and attack angle. If it confirms an injection, it can go further — dropping into an OS command shell, or dumping application usernames/passwords straight off the system. —
— Burp Suite, Arachni, Wapiti, Acunetix, w3af. These are detection-focused, not exploitation-focused: they flag potential vulnerabilities across

categories (not just SQLi) but don't escalate to actually dumping credentials or gaining access. Some are open source, some are paid. These are "dynamic analysis" tools (black-box); the white-box equivalent is "static analysis" tools that review code directly.

The one correct way to prevent SQLi. Construction happens in two separate steps: first the application defines the query structure with placeholders for user-supplied data, then it separately supplies the content of each placeholder. Because the structure is already fixed by the time user input is added, that input can never influence the structure — it's always interpreted as literal data, never as part of the query.
Vulnerable code (user input concatenated directly into the query):
Prepared statements work anywhere untrusted input appears as a
) but not where it needs to name part of the query structure itself — a table or column name, or an
target — since a placeholder can't stand in for that. That's what whitelist validation (below) is for.
Partial Defenses — all last-resort only, never the primary control
defense per the Web Application Hacker's Handbook — usable when there's no alternative, with the understanding it can be bypassed or implemented incorrectly:
— a batch of statements grouped together and stored in the database. Not automatically safe — still has to be called in a parameterized way to actually help.

— define what values are authorized, reject everything else. This is the fallback for exactly the case prepared statements can't cover: a parameter that names part of the query (table/column name) rather than supplying a value.
— should only be used as a last resort.

The idea: make it as difficult as possible for an attacker to compromise the organization by having additional protections in place in case the primary one fails — even with parameterized queries everywhere, if one parameter on one page gets missed, you want the attacker to hit another obstacle before reaching their goal.
Remove or disable any unnecessary default database functionality (including anything that lets the DB execute OS commands or open network connections — the same features Out-of-Band SQLi relies on)
Apply the CIS benchmark for the specific database version in use
Apply all vendor-issued security patches in a timely fashion — the longer a known-vulnerable version stays live, the longer the exploit window

— the application should run against the database with the lowest privilege level possible. If an SQLi vulnerability does lead to remote code execution, the attacker inherits exactly the privilege level the database process runs with — a database running as
hands the attacker the keys immediately; a locked-down service account forces them to work for privilege escalation before they can move laterally.
— as a secondary layer alongside parameterized queries, not instead of them
